items.titel: Jetzt knallt es eben eine Haltestelle weiter

absaetze.t: Am 29. November werden die Stimmberechtigten in der Schweiz über die Feuerwerksinitiative abstimmen. Diese fordert ein landesweites Verbot des Verkaufs und Abbrennens von lauten Feuerwerkskörpern, um die Lärmbelastung für Mensch und Tier zu reduzieren. Grössere, professionelle Feuerwerke, wie zum Beispiel am 1. August oder an anderen öffentlichen Festen, sollen mit einer kantonalen Bewilligung weiterhin durchgeführt werden dürfen.

Die Chancen, dass die Initiative in rund einer Woche angenommen wird, stehen gut. Laut der zweiten SRG-Umfrage des Forschungsinstituts GFS Bern vom 18. November sprechen sich derzeit 63 Prozent der Stimmberechtigten für die Initiative aus, während 35 Prozent dagegen sind. Zwei Prozent sind noch unentschlossen. Im Vergleich zur ersten Umfrage ist die Zustimmung um 6 Prozentpunkte gesunken. Besonders die Anhänger*innen der FDP und SVP tendieren nun mehr zum Nein-Lager.
Verschiebt sich das Problem einfach nach St. Louis und Weil am Rhein?

Rund um Silvester ist das Abbrennen von Feuerwerk in Deutschland und Frankreich grundsätzlich erlaubt. Allerdings gelten in beiden Ländern gewisse zeitliche und örtliche Einschränkungen. So ist Feuerwerk der Kategorie F2 in Deutschland beispielsweise in unmittelbarer Nähe von Krankenhäusern, Pflegeheimen und Kirchen sowie in lokal festgelegten Verbotszonen untersagt.

Für Basel als trinationalen Standort, der geografisch eng mit dem angrenzenden Ausland verbunden ist, stellt die Umsetzung eines Feuerwerksverbots deshalb eine besondere Herausforderung dar. Zwar würde bei einer Annahme der Initiative voraussichtlich auch die bisher geltende zollfreie Einfuhrmenge von 2,5 Kilogramm Feuerwerk aus Deutschland in die Schweiz wegfallen. Nicht verhindern liesse sich jedoch, dass Baslerinnen und Basler ihr Feuerwerk künftig auf der anderen Seite der Landesgrenze kaufen und abbrennen.

Würde privates Feuerwerk in der Schweiz verboten, in den angrenzenden deutschen und französischen Gemeinden wie Weil am Rhein oder Saint-Louis jedoch weiterhin erlaubt bleiben, wäre die Lärmbelastung in der Region demnach keineswegs beseitigt. Zwar reduziert die Distanz den Lärm eines Feuerwerks erheblich, da die Schallenergie mit zunehmender Entfernung abnimmt. Doch gerade in grenznahen Gebieten wie Kleinhüningen oder St. Johann bestünde die Gefahr, dass sich das Problem lediglich über die Landesgrenzen hinweg verlagert.

Dass dies keine rein theoretische Überlegung ist, zeigt ein Beispiel aus den Niederlanden und Belgien: In den Grenzgemeinden Baarle-Nassau (Niederlande) und Baarle-Hertog (Belgien) führten unterschiedliche Feuerwerksregelungen bereits zu einem ausgeprägten Feuerwerkstourismus. Niederländische Konsument*innen wichen auf belgische Geschäfte aus, um Feuerwerk zu kaufen. Die Folgen waren unter anderem Verkehrsprobleme, zusätzliche Belastungen für die Bevölkerung und Schwierigkeiten bei der Kontrolle. Die zuständige grenzüberschreitende Koordinierungsstelle warnte ausdrücklich davor, dass ein niederländisches Feuerwerksverbot diese Probleme auf belgischer Seite noch verschärfen könnte.
Dürfen anderen Ländern keine Vorschriften machen

Manuel Friesecke, Geschäftsführer des Vereins für trinationale Zusammenarbeit Regio Basiliensis, befürchtet deshalb, dass bei einem Feuerwerksverbot in der Schweiz nicht nur die Schweizer Bevölkerung, sondern auch die Menschen im Landkreis Lörrach und im Südelsass von zusätzlichem Lärm betroffen wären. «Es steht uns aber nicht zu, ihnen hier Vorgaben zu machen», sagt Friesecke. Und meint damit, dass es vermessen wäre, Deutschland und Frankreich aufgrund der möglichen Folgen eines Feuerwerksverbots in der Schweiz vorzuschreiben, dass auch dort die Regeln verschärft werden müssten.

Genau ein solches Verbot von Feuerwerk im grenznahen Ausland würde aber der Grünen-Grossrat Harald Friedl begrüssen, welcher gleichermassen auch einsieht,dass es widersprüchlich wäre, wenn beispielsweise im Kanton Basel-Stadt weiterhin ein offizielles Feuerwerk am 31. Juli stattfinden würde, man gleichzeitig aber ein Verbot auf der anderen Seite der Grenze verlangt.

In Deutschland wird auf verschiedenen Ebenen bereits über Einschränkungen von Feuerwerk diskutiert. Eine Annahme der Initiative könnte demnach auch jenseits der Schweizer Grenze neue Impulse für die Debatte geben.

items.titel: UK-EU reset talks will go ‘down to the wire’ as crunch summit approaches
items.anriss: Britain makes concessions on youth mobility scheme as negotiations on food and farming go down to the wire

absaetze.t: British and European negotiators were striving to put the finishing touches to a deal on Thursday night as they provisionally agreed to allow 100,000 EU citizens to come to the UK every year under a new mobility scheme.
The EU-UK reset talks were going “down to the wire”, sources said, as both sides battled over the nature of the UK’s role in shaping future European food and farming rules.

On the eve of a summit in Brussels, the EU was “going into a landing zone” on the question of a British voice in shaping the rules under a food and drink agreement the government hopes to unveil on Friday, an EU source said. The EU compromise emerged in late-night talks on Thursday, after a dispute among member states over how far Britain could be involved in shaping policies related to the food and drink deal.

Earlier on Thursday the UK made concessions to increase the quota of EU citizens who could take part in a new youth mobility scheme, agreeing a cap of 100,000, instead of 50,000-80,0000 as previously sought.
It was also agreed to raise the age cap from 30 to 31.

The number of young British people allowed to go to the EU under the scheme will be matched but could be higher, with some countries, including Germany, being prepared to take unlimited numbers each year.

With less than 24 hours to go before Andy Burnham was due in Brussels for the summit with EU leaders, the two sides still needed to resolve some central sticking points, including how much of a say Britain will have in new EU food rules.

Speaking in general terms about the disagreements, also including tuition fees for EU students in the UK, another EU diplomat said: “It will go down to the wire. Our feeling is that the Brits have to move if they want a deal.”

A spokesperson for the British prime minister also described the talks as close, saying if an agreement was reached, the government would bring forward legislation, the cutting costs bill, to parliament next week.
Another EU diplomat said ambassadors representing the EU member states would meet at 5pm and “will go until agreement is reached tonight”.
Sources said the UK was still resisting pressure from the EU on tuition fees for EU students coming to Britain under the youth mobility scheme.
“We are fighting hard on this and think we will get there,” said an EU insider. “But for us, one of the hardest discussions centres on this question of the UK being a rule taker or rule maker.”

At the long-awaited summit, the EU and UK hope to sign three agreements, which are expected to add 0.4% to British GDP, including the including a highly prized food and drink deal that was a Labour manifesto commitment.
The deal, expected to come into force on 1 March 2028, requires the UK to align with EU rules on sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) standards, making Britain a rule taker.

Asked about Britain’s status as a rule taker, No 10 said the Labour manifesto had aimed to build closer ties with the EU, adding: “We were obviously elected on a manifesto that promised to reset the relationship and seek to deepen ties with our European friends.”
According to EU sources, the UK has been pushing to have a formal role in EU committees involved in implementing existing and setting new SPS rules.
An EU diplomat said: “They want to be able to shape decisions, not only implementation, but future decisions. That has always been a red line.”
Under the SPS proposal, the UK will agree to dynamically align with EU laws and will have a “voice” but “not be in the room” when laws are drafted.
A second diplomat from a country sympathetic to the British position said the European Commission had proposed an “extremely restrictive consultation mechanism” for the UK.
In contrast, the EU diplomat thought it was reasonable for a British representative to take part in the implementation of SPS legislation affecting the UK.
“Of course the UK cannot vote in the council as a non-member state, but we feel that we need to be pragmatic about coordination and implementation,” they said.

The issue proved difficult to resolve because it divided member states. France was perceived by other member states to be the main barrier to greater UK involvement in EU working groups on food and drink laws. “They are super principled on that point,” said a second EU diplomat.
The French government does not agree that it has been the main block, arguing that only a few member states wanted to accommodate the UK.
The issue raises the tensions at the heart of the UK’s status as a rule taker, and would be many times magnified were Britain to choose to enter the single market as a non-EU member state.
The precise details of how the UK would be consulted on future food and farming rules remain unclear.
Separately, the EU and UK remain deadlocked over whether EU students in Britain should pay the British or international tuition fee rate.
The draft proposal gives the UK two options: to agree to significantly reduced undergraduate fees or equal treatment with nationals.

Burnham’s spokesperson suggested there was an UK-EU consensus that there would be no further incremental reset summits beyond the one on Friday until a full negotiation commenced on a longer-term, more stable relationship, such as rejoining the single market.
“After the summit, we will begin those discussions with our European partners about the realistic options for our longer-term relationship,” he said.

The UK has prioritised seeking commitments on Britain’s position relating to the EU’s Made in Europe legislation. The trade defence policy will include tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles but will also affect British manufacturing. The sides are believed to be close to an agreement to language at the summit that would point towards UK inclusion, but nothing can be formalised until the EU passes its own legislation.

Burnham’s spokesperson said: “[The UK is] engaging constructively with the EU on that, and we’ve been clear about the challenges it could represent for British industries. We have deeply integrated supply chains with Europe, and we want to keep working together to boost growth and open up trade.
“The UK and Europe have shared economic challenges, and we believe shared challenges are best met with a collective approach that is in Britain’s best interests, and in Europe’s too.”

items.titel: UK and EU plan first talks on sending refused asylum seekers to third countries
items.anriss: Two sides to commit to discussing third-country hubs as part of reset pact after five-country deal with Rwanda

absaetze.t: The UK and the EU plan to establish formal talks for the first time about sending rejected asylum seekers to third-country hubs, according to a leaked document.

A draft of a joint statement expected to be signed by Andy Burnham and Ursula von der Leyen at a summit on Friday morning states that both sides will establish “a structured dialogue” to discuss “returns to third countries”.
Until now, the Home Office has been seeking bilateral agreements with third countries allowing the removal of migrants, but with no obvious success.
Last week, five EU countries – Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands – announced an agreement in principle with Rwanda to establish a migrant “return hub” there in 2027.

Burnham hinted at possible cooperation with EU countries last week when he told reporters that the UK had not had direct discussions with European governments involved in return hubs but “we will watch that [the five-country deal] with interest, learning from what went on in the past”. He said: “The public want us to do whatever we can to deal with illegal immigration.”
The UK has been fighting for deeper cooperation with the EU on migration, with the new deal on a “strategic dialogue” secured in the last two weeks by negotiators in Brussels.

It is a key part of the UK-EU reset pact, which also covers a youth mobility scheme, tariffs on Chinese imports, food and drink exports to the EU and a wider restatement of commitment on defence and security.
Informed sources confirmed this was the first time the UK and the EU had agreed to “open a dialogue on returns” after the launch of the bloc’s Channel action plan in June this year.
Whitehall sources said the UK was now open to the possibility of sending rejected claimants to Rwanda – a recent pivot from the position under Keir Starmer’s government, which rejected the move.
According to a draft of the joint agreement, negotiations over third-country hubs will be part of increased cooperation to tackle irregular migration.

The document states: “The EU and UK … will establish a structured dialogue on migration covering in particular the joint activities under the Channel action plan, action against irregular migration and migrant smuggling networks, strategic communication and border management, upstream cooperation and engagement with third countries, returns to third countries, pull factors for irregular migrants and legal pathway.”
In May, the UK and 45 other European countries signed an agreement that explicitly endorsed plans to send unwanted asylum seekers to third-country hubs.

A political declaration from the 46 members of the Council of Europe, the body that oversees the European convention on human rights (ECHR), said states had an “undeniable sovereign right” to control their borders.

It is understood that the UK has been seeking a deal with an unnamed third country, similar to the Italy-Albania agreement that allowed Rome to place detention centres in Albania. Albania has ruled out a bilateral agreement on a return hub with the UK.

Previous discussions have reportedly centred on 11 countries: Armenia, Egypt, Ethiopia, Ghana, Libya, Mauritania, Rwanda, Senegal, Tunisia, Uganda and Uzbekistan. Montenegro has denied reports that it is considering housing refused asylum seekers.
Starmer scrapped a Tory plan to forcibly send small-boat arrivals to Rwanda where their asylum claims would have been processed.

Before the election, the Conservative government had spent £700m on its Rwanda returns policy, which was meant to deter Channel crossings. The scheme hit legal and political obstacles from the start, with the UK supreme court eventually ruling it illegal.

Under Burnham, the Home Office has refused to close down the possibility of sending asylum seekers to Rwanda. This week, when asked if the UK might ever send asylum seekers to Rwanda, a Home Office spokesperson said: “The UK, like other European countries, is exploring innovative approaches including returns hubs to tackle illegal migration.”
The UK has been looking for years to strengthen cooperation with France and other EU member states to tackle small boats carrying asylum seekers across the Channel.

But sources say it is only in recent months that there has been a change of mood in the EU, with member states realising that the intensity of criminal trafficking across the Channel is “proving [to be] a pull factor” to enter the EU. Those that fail to make it to British shores remain in the EU’s migrant support system.

Responding to the planned cooperation on migrant hubs, Madeleine Sumption, the head of the Migration Observatory at Oxford University, said: “Its inclusion in the statement would confirm the now relatively widespread interest in ‘third country’ options.”
In response, Imran Hussain, the director of external affairs at the Refugee Council, said return hubs were likely to be difficult and costly to run.
“Removing people to places they have never stepped foot will be difficult and distressing,” he said.
“The last decade has shown that working with people to support their return to their countries is far more successful.”

A Home Office spokesperson said: “While we are not part of this EU member state initiative, there is widespread international agreement on the need to have practical and workable solutions to deal with the global challenge of illegal migration.

“We continue to explore innovative approaches, including returns hubs, to build on the 80,000 people with no right to be in the UK returned or deported since July 2024. We have consistently made clear that we support the principle of returns hubs.”

items.titel: Italy’s hard definition of antisemitism will shield Israeli crimes and harm free speech
items.anriss: Anti-Jewish discrimination and legitimate criticism of Israeli state actions became conflated into one offence by Italy’s parliament on Tuesday (17 November).

absaetze.t: Anti-Jewish discrimination and legitimate criticism of Israeli state actions became conflated into one offence by Italy’s parliament on Tuesday (17 November).

Adopting the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance’s (IHRA) official definition of anti-semitism, Rome’s bill will apply across schools, universities, social-media platforms, and beyond. The move has raised serious concerns about what this will do to freedom of expression and protest.
Despite not imposing financial penalties or criminal sanctions for offenders, it shows which side of history far-right prime minister Georgia Meloni’s Italy has chosen.

“Branding criticism of Israel’s brutal occupation, its system of apartheid, and its ongoing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza as antisemitic – which could happen under the new law – also risks shielding state policies and practices from legitimate public scrutiny and debate,” said Erika Guevara Rosas, Amnesty International’s senior director for policy and research.
“By blurring the distinction between antisemitism and criticism of a state’s actions, the law also risks undermining efforts to identify and effectively address genuine antisemitisms,” she said.

Not only does Tuesday mark a bleak beginning for press and self-censorship on issues of public interest in Italy, following the path of the UK’s persecution of the Palestine Action group, who has now arrested over 4,000 activists involved in peaceful protests against Israel’s offences in the occupied territories.

Not only does this also indicate the start of an authoritarian slippery slope, which could end in silencing political criticism that is not favoured by the ruling powers, or debate concerning those in office.
But it is largely a display of the narrow priorities subscribed to by Meloni’s stagnant government.

Although she has held power for longer than any of her predecessors in the history of the Republic, there is little to show for it, with headline measures that included tightened citizenship rules, anti-rave actions, cuts to welfare benefits, and limited offshoring of migrant processing to an exorbitantly expensive centre in Albania.
And stalled economic growth matches the trend.

Meanwhile, in a 147-93 vote in Rome’s Palazzo Chigi, supporters of the pro-IHRA definition bill cited soaring anti-Jewish violence and aggression as their main motivation, while forgetting about the abundant relics of fascism that still scar whole cities and regions across Italy, influencing every generation with hatred of minorities.

Even the granddaughter of Italy’s late fascist dictator, Rachele Mussolini, has quit Meloni's Brothers of Italy party for being too rightwing in its treatment of minorities, which should speak volumes on the government's lack of integrity in its claims to care about Jewish people in Italy.

As repression increasingly hits press and NGO freedoms in Europe and beyond, laws that seek to police the vocabulary of crucial democratic debates risk pushing our societies back into dark times, which our grandparents fought to end.

In 2024, the German parliament passed a non-binding resolution backing the IHRA definition. Two years later, Germany is considering a law that would make denying Israel’s right to exist a crime, with up to five years in prison.

items.titel: Pourquoi Shenzhen n’est pas un second Yalta
items.anriss: Je ne pense pas que cette analogie soit très pertinente ; elle détourne l’attention. En 1945, les trois Alliés avaient combattu ensemble les puissances de l’Axe et devaient encore unir leurs forces pour vaincre le Japon. Ils étaient déjà …

absaetze.t: Testez le Grand Continent. Les idées et les analyses qu’on ne trouve nulle part. Mais que vous verrez bientôt partout. Dans votre boîte mail à partir de 8 euros par mois

Dans votre livre Making the World Again 1, vous racontez comment Churchill, Roosevelt et Staline ont bâti la paix au sortir de la guerre. Après la rencontre entre Trump, Xi et Poutine à Shenzhen, assistons-nous à l’émergence de nouveaux « Trois Grands », ou cette analogie est-elle trompeuse ?

Je ne pense pas que cette analogie soit très pertinente ; elle détourne l’attention. En 1945, les trois Alliés avaient combattu ensemble les puissances de l’Axe et devaient encore unir leurs forces pour vaincre le Japon. Ils étaient déjà parvenus à certains accords sur l’avenir de l’Europe, ce qui ressemble peut-être un peu à ce que la Russie aimerait proposer aujourd’hui. Moscou s’emploie manifestement à accréditer l’idée d’un second Yalta, où les grandes puissances se réunissent et décident du sort de l’Europe sans que les Européens aient leur mot à dire.

Mais l’Europe est très différente aujourd’hui. Les trois puissances qui se réunissent en Chine ne sont d’ailleurs en aucun cas des alliées. Et la Russie n’est pas une grande puissance : elle s’est gravement affaiblie à cause de la guerre en Ukraine et dépend désormais beaucoup plus de la Chine. Les Russes voudraient nous faire croire que c’est tout simplement ainsi que se comportent les grandes puissances.
Qu’est-ce qui pourrait unir trois pays qui sont le plus souvent en concurrence ?

La Russie et la Chine entretiennent des liens – Poutine s’est rendu en Chine à cinq reprises ces dernières années et a donc souvent rencontré Xi Jinping. Mais il existe des tensions historiques : au XIXe siècle, la Russie s’est emparée de nombreux territoires que la Chine considérait comme siens, et au XXe siècle, notamment du vivant de Mao, les relations se sont fortement dégradées. Elles n’ont donc pas toujours été amicales. En raison de la guerre en Ukraine, les Russes sont désormais beaucoup plus dépendants de la Chine ; ils font clairement figure de partenaire de second rang.

Entre les États-Unis et la Chine, il existe des tensions qui vont perdurer. Ce qui est envisageable, c’est que ces trois puissances parviennent à une sorte d’entente. Elle ne sera pas consignée par écrit, mais il pourrait y avoir un accord tacite sur les sphères d’influence : la Chine partira du principe qu’elle peut dominer son voisinage, la Russie tentera de dominer l’Eurasie, et les États-Unis – ou du moins le président Trump – souhaiteraient dominer l’hémisphère occidental. Il a évoqué une « doctrine Donroe », visant à préserver l’hémisphère occidental de toute ingérence extérieure. C’est donc possible, mais je ne vois aucune véritable amitié ni alliance entre ces trois pays. Ils partagent certes certaines façons d’agir et des objectifs de même nature, mais cela n’a rien à voir avec une alliance nouée pour faire la guerre.
Dans Nixon and Mao 2, vous décriviez comment Washington jouait Pékin contre Moscou pendant la guerre froide. Ce triangle s’est-il inversé, et au profit de qui ?

Je pense que c’est désormais la Chine qui joue les États-Unis et la Russie l’un contre l’autre. Xi Jinping aimerait beaucoup être perçu comme l’homme d’État modéré. L’image qu’il veut donner, c’est celle où il se tient au milieu, entre Trump et Poutine : la Chine au centre du jeu. Il s’est montré très prudent. Il a soutenu la Russie dans une certaine mesure – la Chine lui a fourni des renseignements et lui a vendu des armes – mais Pékin s’est tenu légèrement en retrait de la guerre en Ukraine et a choisi de ne pas s’impliquer directement, ce qui en dit long. Dans le même temps, Xi est disposé à dialoguer avec Trump. La Chine se trouve donc au sommet du triangle.

Les nationalistes chinois considèrent Shenzhen comme le signe d’une capitulation américaine et de la fin de l’hégémonie des États-Unis. S’agit-il simplement d’une posture, ou y a-t-il quelque chose qui échappe aux commentateurs occidentaux ?

D’une certaine manière, Trump a capitulé, car il traite Poutine comme un ami très cher. Le langage corporel est révélateur : il a posé sa main sur le bras de Poutine, lui a serré la main et a répété qu’il était un grand ami. Pour Poutine, c’est être reconnu comme un homme d’État de premier plan. Il a été mis au ban ces dernières années en raison de son invasion de l’Ukraine, et ce sommet lui permet de revenir sur le devant de la scène. Il est difficile de trouver un précédent à un tel sommet.
En quel sens ?

Les sommets ont toujours porté sur des questions épineuses, mais il ne s’agit ici ni d’une véritable discussion ni d’une négociation. Nous ne connaissons pas l’ordre du jour et rien ne dit qu’il ait été sérieusement préparé. Normalement, lorsque des chefs d’État se réunissent pour négocier, la rencontre est préparée des mois à l’avance. Celle-ci ne l’a pas été, et il est très difficile de savoir si elle mènera vraiment quelque part.

Téhéran, Yalta et Potsdam par le passé ; aujourd’hui, la villa Kylin, une résidence au bord d’un lac à Shenzhen, où Xi reçoit en maître des lieux. Faut-il lire ce choix diplomatique comme un signal géopolitique ?

Nous assistons à une diplomatie au coup par coup. Les Chinois se sont très bien préparés, et Poutine est venu avec une liste d’exigences, mais on ne sait absolument pas ce que veulent les États-Unis. Des réunions sans ordre du jour me semblent relever davantage de l’improvisation que d’une négociation sérieuse.

Les chefs d’État adorent les sommets. Ils s’y sentent importants : les fanfares jouent, on les acclame – Xi Jinping a accueilli Trump en musique et en danse. Ils échappent ainsi à leurs problèmes et à la politique intérieure. Mais ces sommets aboutissent-ils vraiment à grand-chose ?

Ce qui permet vraiment d’aboutir à des accords internationaux, ce sont des négociations âpres et difficiles. Elles peuvent prendre beaucoup de temps et exigent des experts, des personnes qui maîtrisent réellement le sujet. On ne négocie pas à la légère une réduction des arsenaux nucléaires : il y a tant de détails techniques à comprendre – les vecteurs, le type de bombe – et il faut mettre en place des inspections, comme cela a été fait pour les grands accords de contrôle des armements des années 1970 et 1980. Je ne vois guère de signe de cela aujourd’hui.
Des réunions comme celle-ci se prêtent à la propagande, et Moscou s’efforce de manipuler l’opinion publique européenne sur la situation en Ukraine. Comment en rendre compte de manière lucide ?

Nous devons souligner ce qui ne s’est pas produit. Il y a les séances photo, Trump déclare déjà que c’était « la meilleure réunion de tous les temps » et qu’il adore Poutine et Xi Jinping. Ce que nous devons faire, c’est demander : qu’est-ce qui a concrètement été obtenu ? Qu’est-ce qui a réellement changé ? Pourquoi le présenter comme un grand triomphe ? Comme dit l’adage, le diable se cache dans les détails : c’est là qu’il faut regarder. Je ne pense pas qu’il en sortira un accord majeur qui nous fasse vraiment avancer ou qui rende réellement le monde plus serein.
Roosevelt pensait pouvoir « gérer » Staline en misant sur une relation personnelle. Lorsque Trump qualifie Xi et Poutine d’amis, se berce-t-il de la même illusion ?

Trump a toujours cru aux relations personnelles. Roosevelt a surestimé sa propre capacité à gagner Staline à ses vues, mais il servait une cause plus haute : il voulait bâtir une Organisation des Nations unies qui préviendrait les guerres futures. Il y a consacré une énergie considérable, et la mise en place de la structure de l’ONU ainsi que des institutions de Bretton Woods – le Fonds monétaire international et la Banque mondiale – a demandé un travail colossal. L’objectif, comme l’énonce la Charte des Nations unies, était de débarrasser le monde du fléau de la guerre. Roosevelt savait que Staline n’était pas un démocrate – ce n’était un secret pour personne –, mais il espérait travailler avec lui et faire entrer l’Union soviétique dans la communauté des nations. Et Staline était disposé à rejoindre les Nations unies, convaincu que cela servirait les intérêts de l’Union soviétique. En 1945, l’Union soviétique était la plus grande puissance militaire d’Europe, mais elle avait été durement éprouvée par la guerre. Elle avait besoin de se reconstruire et, pour autant que nous puissions en juger, Staline était prêt à collaborer pacifiquement avec les autres nations. Je ne vois rien de tel aujourd’hui.
Et Trump, que cherche-t-il à obtenir ?

Je ne vois pas quelle est la vision du monde de Trump. À l’instar de Roosevelt, il pense pouvoir rallier n’importe qui en le charmant et en lui donnant des tapes dans le dos. Et il a une approche purement transactionnelle : il cherche à savoir ce que Poutine et Xi veulent, ou ne veulent pas, et il conclut un accord. C’est ainsi qu’il semble concevoir la politique étrangère. Pour autant que l’on puisse en juger, il n’écoute pas ses conseillers et il a vidé de sa substance le département d’État, où de nombreuses personnes ont été licenciées. Apparemment, ses couloirs sont désormais vides. Il ne cherche pas à construire un autre monde. Il cherche à conclure des accords, en partant du principe que tout le monde a un prix.

Dans leur déclaration, les trois dirigeants se sont engagés à réformer les Nations unies. Assistons-nous aujourd’hui au démantèlement de cet héritage de la Seconde Guerre mondiale par la puissance même qui l’a conçu ?

Les États-Unis ont joué un rôle clef dans la création des Nations unies. En 1945, ils étaient la première puissance économique mondiale ainsi qu’une grande puissance militaire – plus forts, en réalité, que l’Union soviétique, qui était une puissance militaire mais pas économique. La Grande-Bretagne venait nettement en troisième position, car elle commençait à perdre son empire. Il y a toujours eu des tensions et des problèmes avec Washington, mais les États-Unis, qui avaient été le principal soutien des Nations unies et de l’idée que les nations peuvent œuvrer ensemble pour la paix, sont désormais devenus un fauteur de troubles.

Trump a clairement fait savoir qu’il n’avait pas une très haute opinion des Nations unies ; il les traite avec mépris. Il aime y prononcer des discours, mais celui qu’il y a tenu cette année ne portait pas vraiment sur la paix mondiale. Il a surtout insisté sur le fait qu’il n’avait pas perdu l’élection – une diatribe, d’ailleurs assez déprimante. Même s’ils ont commis des erreurs et parfois ignoré l’ordre international, les États-Unis avaient soutenu cet ordre pratiquement sans interruption depuis 1945. Sous Trump – lors de son premier mandat et plus encore lors de son second – la situation a basculé. Ils ont réduit leur soutien à des institutions telles que l’Organisation mondiale de la santé, qui fait partie du système des Nations unies, et se sont repliés sur eux-mêmes : Trump parle de défendre les intérêts américains. La question pour l’avenir est de savoir s’il sera possible de reconstruire une forme d’organisation internationale, et si une autre administration américaine s’y emploiera. Il y a deux difficultés. Les États-Unis ont affaibli leur propre capacité à mener leur diplomatie et à collaborer avec d’autres nations, et ils se sont aliéné de nombreux alliés de longue date.

items.titel: L'agenda européen : les principaux événements prévus du 23 au 29 novembre 2026
items.anriss: Lundi 23 novembre , les ministres chargés des aides régionales doivent adopter des conclusions sur les régions ultrapériphériques de l' UE , dont plusieurs territoires français d'outre-mer, les Açores et les Canaries. Le texte doit …

absaetze.t: Le prochain budget européen, l'aide à l'Ukraine et les élections législatives espagnoles dominent la semaine. À Strasbourg, les eurodéputés voteront plusieurs textes, tandis que la Commission présentera ses nouvelles orientations économiques. Les dirigeants européens tenteront également de s'accorder sur les dépenses de l'UE après 2027.

Lundi 23 novembre, les ministres chargés des aides régionales doivent adopter des conclusions sur les régions ultrapériphériques de l'UE, dont plusieurs territoires français d'outre-mer, les Açores et les Canaries. Le texte doit préciser les priorités européennes pour ces territoires confrontés à l'éloignement géographique, aux coûts de transport élevés et aux risques climatiques.

Lundi 23 novembre, les ministres européens de l'Agriculture et de la Pêche examinent les propositions de quotas de pêche pour 2027 dans l'Atlantique, la mer du Nord et la Méditerranée. Leurs échanges doivent préparer un accord en décembre sur les quantités de poissons que chaque pays sera autorisé à capturer.

Mardi 24 novembre, le Parlement européen, réuni à Strasbourg, doit voter plusieurs textes visant à alléger les obligations administratives des entreprises. Les eurodéputés se prononceront sur l'accélération des évaluations environnementales de certains projets et l'extension de règles simplifiées aux petites entreprises de taille intermédiaire.

Mardi 24 novembre, la Commission européenne prévoit de présenter une proposition législative sur les technologies quantiques, destinées notamment à développer des ordinateurs très puissants et des systèmes de communication sécurisés. Elle souhaite faciliter le financement de la recherche et la production industrielle en Europe, face à la concurrence américaine et chinoise.

Mardi 24 novembre, la Commission doit également publier le paquet d'automne du Semestre européen, son exercice annuel de surveillance économique. Elle évaluera les projets de budgets nationaux pour 2027, leur conformité aux règles européennes et les risques de dérapage des déficits publics.

Mercredi 25 novembre, les eurodéputés doivent voter plusieurs textes sur les médicaments, visant notamment à prévenir les pénuries et à faciliter l'accès aux traitements dans l'UE. Ils doivent également se prononcer sur le budget européen pour 2027, afin de confirmer le compromis négocié avec les États membres.

Mercredi 25 novembre, les dirigeants de l'UE et des Balkans occidentaux se retrouvent à Bruxelles pour faire le point sur leur rapprochement. Le sommet portera sur les réformes attendues des pays candidats et les aides européennes destinées à soutenir leurs économies avant une éventuelle adhésion.

Jeudi 26 et vendredi 27 novembre, les dirigeants des Vingt-Sept se réunissent pour un Conseil européen extraordinaire consacré au prochain budget de l'UE pour 2028-2034. Ils chercheront à rapprocher leurs positions sur le financement des aides agricoles, des régions et des nouvelles priorités européennes. Le soutien financier à l'Ukraine en 2027 figure également à l'ordre du jour, alors que Kiev reste largement dépendante du soutien de ses partenaires.

Jeudi 26 novembre, un sommet de la zone euro réunit les dirigeants des pays partageant la monnaie unique. Ils discuteront de la situation économique et des finances publiques. La succession de Christine Lagarde à la présidence de la BCE pourrait également être abordée, après l'annonce de son départ anticipé pour le 7 février 2027.

Dimanche 29 novembre, les nouvelles normes automobiles Euro 7 commencent à s'appliquer aux nouveaux modèles de voitures et de véhicules utilitaires légers soumis à homologation. Elles renforcent notamment les exigences concernant les particules émises par les freins et la durée de vie des batteries. Les règles s'étendront à l'ensemble des véhicules neufs concernés un an plus tard.

Dimanche 29 novembre, l'Espagne organise des élections législatives anticipées, après la dissolution du Parlement décidée par le Premier ministre socialiste Pedro Sánchez. Les électeurs renouvellent les 350 sièges du Congrès des députés, élus à la proportionnelle par province, ainsi que le Sénat. Le Parti populaire (PP), conservateur, affronte notamment le PSOE de Pedro Sánchez et Vox, formation d'extrême droite.

items.titel: In Dutzenden Städten: Jugendproteste in ganz Deutschland
items.anriss: In Dutzenden Städten sind Proteste angekündigt. Unter anderem die Bundesschülerkonferenz, "Schulstreik gegen die Wehrpflicht", "Gen Z regelt" und Fridays For Future haben heute bundesweit zu Demonstrationen aufgerufen. [ mehr ]

absaetze.t: In Dutzenden Städten sind Proteste angekündigt. Unter anderem die Bundesschülerkonferenz, "Schulstreik gegen die Wehrpflicht", "Gen Z regelt" und Fridays For Future haben bundesweit zu Demonstrationen aufgerufen.

Heute mobilisieren bundes- und europaweit verschiedene Gruppen zum gemeinsamen Jugendprotest. Mit der Initiative "Gen Z regelt" ruft dabei in Deutschland ein dezentral organisiertes Netzwerk ebenso zur Teilnahme auf wie die Schüler-Gruppe "Schulstreik gegen Wehrpflicht", die bereits mehrfach bundesweit demonstriert hatte. Zur Generation Z zählen, grob gesagt, die von 1995 bis 2010 Geborenen. Auch die Bundesschülerkonferenz plant in Berlin eine Demonstration.

Nicht alle Anliegen werden von den Demonstrierenden geteilt, oft haben sie unterschiedliche Ziele. Auf der Webseite von "Gen Z regelt" werden sechs zentrale Forderungen genannt: Sie treten ein für bessere Bildung, gegen steigende Lebenshaltungskosten und eine ungerechte Lastenverteilung.

Zudem sprechen sie sich gegen Überwachung, für mehr Klimaschutz und gegen die Wehrpflicht aus. Beim letzten Punkt gibt es eine Schnittmenge zu den streikenden Schülerinnen und Schülern, die sich unter dem Motto "Fight for our Future - not their wars" gegen Wehrpflicht und Musterung aussprechen.
Bundesbildungsministerin verspricht politische Einbindung

Bundesbildungsministerin Karin Prien verspricht auf berechtigte Interessen einzugehen. Sie möchte junge Menschen in "politische Entscheidungen einbeziehen". Und: "Unsere dringendste Aufgabe ist Generationengerechtigkeit und dabei muss Bildung Priorität haben." Für Bildung investierten Bund und Länder aber auch bereits erheblich.

Bei den von "Gen Z regelt" organisierten Protesten am 31. Oktober waren bundesweit Zehntausende weitgehend friedlich auf die Straße gegangen. Danach gab es abends in mehreren Städten vereinzelt Ausschreitungen, etwa in Frankfurt am Main. Damals hatte "Gen Z regelt" nach eigenen Angaben mehr als 180.000 Anmeldungen bundesweit.
Bundeskanzler Merz, der bei den Demonstrationen aktiv kritisiert wurde, ließ damals über seinen Sprecher mitteilen, dass junge Menschen "legitime Anliegen" verträten, die er "sehr ernst" nehme.

items.titel: Asia’s stock markets dive as Anthropic debut fails to allay AI bubble fears
items.anriss: Indexes in Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Hong Kong fall amid tech sell-off.

absaetze.t: Indexes in Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Hong Kong fall amid tech sell-off.
Asian stock markets have opened to steep losses as fears that the AI boom is unsustainable continue to weigh on sentiment despite Anthropic’s blockbuster debut.

Markets in Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Hong Kong fell sharply on Friday, as investor excitement around the AI giant’s public listing failed to ally concerns about the sustainability of the multi-trillion-dollar investments propping up the sector.
Tokyo’s benchmark Nikkei 225 and Seoul’s Kospi each tumbled about 4.5 percent in morning trading, while the Taiex in Taipei plunged nearly 6 percent.
Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index dipped as much as 2 percent.
The sell-off reflects concerns that AI-led growth is slowing down and the “peak growth phase” may have passed, said Rajat Agarwal, an Asia equity strategist with Societe Generale.
“The second element is on the demand vacuum that we are seeing,” Agarwal told Al Jazeera.
“At the time when foreigners are not buying, it is to be seen how long can the domestic investors stay put, particularly in Korea, on which the drawdown has been more severe.”
Like Wall Street, Asia’s main bourses are heavily exposed to AI.

The region is home to some of the key players in the global AI ecosystem, including South Korean memory chip makers SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, Taiwanese contract chipmaker TSMC, and Japanese investment holding company Softbank Group.
Tech firms have poured trillions of dollars into AI in recent year, stoking fears of a speculative market bubble similar to the one that preceded the 2000 dot-com crash.
Global AI-related investment is projected to reach $2.7 trillion in 2026 and $3.6 trillion in 2027, according to technology insights company Gartner.

Market sentiment has been further dampened by moves in Washington to clampdown on China’s access to advanced chips amid claims that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was romantically involved with a Chinese intelligence operative or asset.

The US Bureau of Industry and Security this week announced new export licence requirements aimed at preventing Chinese AI developers from remotely accessing top-of-the-line compute power at data centres in third countries, mainly in Southeast Asia,
The market retreat in Asia followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, even as Anthropic shares jumped 17 percent on their first day of trading on the Nasdaq stock exchange in New York.
Anthrophic’s stock price rose as high as $111 before settling just about $97, vaulting the Claude creator into the ranks of the world’s most valuable companies.
The San Francisco-based AI giant’s market debut came after it raised $81.3bn in the largest initial public offering (IPO) in history, leapfrogging the previous record of $75bn set by SpaceX in June.
Despite the excitement around Anthrophic, key indexes closed in the red, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite dropping 2.3 percent and the broader S&P500 falling 2 percent.

items.titel: Washington délivre ses premiers permis d'extraction minière en haute mer, dans le Pacifique
items.anriss: Le gouvernement de Donald Trump a annoncé jeudi avoir délivré ses premiers permis d'extraction minière en haute mer, dans le Pacifique, malgré une décision de justice défavorable et l'inquiétude des défenseurs de l'environnement.

absaetze.t: Le gouvernement de Donald Trump a annoncé jeudi avoir délivré ses premiers permis d'extraction minière en haute mer, dans le Pacifique, malgré une décision de justice défavorable et l'inquiétude des défenseurs de l'environnement.

Les deux permis couvrent plus de 125'000 kilomètres carrés – l'équivalent de plus de 20% du territoire français – près des Samoa américaines, des territoires sous la souveraineté de Washington dans le sud-ouest du Pacifique.

"C'est la première fois que les États-Unis ont organisé la vente de permis d'exploitation offshore de minéraux critiques pour le Pacifique, une étape historique pour la sécurité énergétique et minérale" du pays, a écrit dans un communiqué Doug Burgum, le ministre américain en charge du dossier.
Les deux permis ont été soldés pour un total de 6 millions de dollars en faveur d'entreprises dont les noms n'ont pas été publiés.
Cette autorisation suit le soutien de Donald Trump à cette industrie naissante et très critiquée.

Le président américain avait pris en avril 2025 un décret pour permettre l'exploitation minière des fonds marins en remettant en cause l'Autorité internationale des fonds marins (AIFM), théoriquement compétente en haute mer. Une décision critiquée, des associations environnementales au gouvernement chinois.

La décision de jeudi doit permettre "d'en apprendre davantage sur les ressources au large des côtes des Samoa américaines et d'évaluer si elles pourraient contribuer à un approvisionnement national plus fiable", a affirmé le ministre Doug Burgum.
Espèces protégées
Les fonds marins sont convoités pour leur richesse en minéraux très demandés pour les véhicules électriques, les smartphones et ordinateurs portables, ou encore les panneaux solaires.
Mais les scientifiques s'inquiètent des risques environnementaux liés à l'exploitation minière, et des dizaines de pays plaident pour un moratoire.

Aux Samoa américaines, les autorités locales ont interdit en 2024 l'exploitation du sous-sol océanique dans les eaux dont elles ont la souveraineté, mais le gouvernement fédéral a autorité au-delà, sur la zone externe du plateau continental concernée par ces nouveaux permis.
Lundi, un juge fédéral de Hawaï, saisi par des opposants, a estimé que le gouvernement avait enfreint la loi dans la procédure d'attribution de ces permis.
L'agence fédérale concernée "n'a même pas essayé de prendre en considération les effets potentiels" du projet sur les espèces de faune et de flore protégées, a écrit le juge.
La zone, près de l'aire marine protégée de Rose Atoll, abrite de nombreuses espèces protégées dont des baleines, des tortues, des requins et des coraux.

L'octroi de ces permis jeudi malgré la décision de justice constitue ainsi un "acte rebelle et illégal", a tonné un avocat de l'association environnementale Earthjustice, promettant de tout faire pour annuler ces autorisations.

items.titel: Meta rethinks 2030 climate goals as AI data centres drive emissions up
items.anriss: Rising data centre energy needs force Meta to review sustainability targets amid growing corporate climate retreat.

absaetze.t: Rising data center energy needs force Meta to adjust its sustainability targets amid growing corporate climate retreat.

Meta, the owner of Facebook and Instagram, has said it is reconsidering its 2030 deadline for reaching net-zero emissions because of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, in the latest sign of a broad corporate retreat from climate pledges.

The company is “re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing and interim milestones, including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal”, Rachel Peterson, Meta’s vice president of data centres, and Blair Swedeen, its global head of net zero and sustainability, said in the company’s annual sustainability report on Thursday.
Meta reported that its net carbon-equivalent emissions rose 45 percent in 2025 to 11.8 million tonnes, a figure that is itself based on accounting methods that climate advocates view with scepticism.

“When we set our net zero emissions goal, we anticipated steady growth, falling clean energy costs, and changes in the broader system that would enable progress at the pace we envisioned. The reality has been far more complex,” the executives wrote in the report. They said delivering on Meta’s vision “requires building the infrastructure that powers AI”.
What was the pledge?

In 2020, Meta set a goal of net-zero emissions across its entire value chain by 2030, in line with the Paris Agreement, which aims to hold long-term warming to 1.5C (2.7F) above pre-industrial levels.

Net zero means eliminating emissions as far as possible and buying credits from carbon removal projects to offset those that cannot be eliminated. The value chain covers emissions from sources such as purchased goods and services, as well as capital goods such as equipment, buildings and vehicles.

A study published this week in the journal Nature Sustainability found that 403 of the most powerful data centres in the United States accounted for about 2 percent of the country’s electricity use and a carbon footprint comparable to Denmark’s, the AFP news agency reported.

About 1,200 such “hyperscale” data centres are online, and hundreds more are planned. Globally, data centres used about 415 terawatt hours of electricity in 2024, about 1.5 percent of supply, and that could nearly double by 2030, according to the International Energy Agency.
A wider retreat
During US President Donald Trump’s second term, major American businesses have stepped back from environmental commitments.
The trend is not confined to Big Tech. General Motors, which set a goal of selling only zero-emission vehicles by 2035, backed the Trump administration’s weakening of a fuel economy rule this year.
Walmart acknowledged in 2024 that it would miss its first emissions target. Google, which pledged in 2020 to run on carbon-free energy by 2030, said this year that its emissions were still rising.
Coca-Cola and Pepsi have changed the baseline years for their emissions targets and weakened their ambitions.

items.titel: The Jet That Always Shadows Air Force One When The President Travels Abroad
items.anriss: U.S. President Donald Trump’s recent visit to China has drawn particular attention from online flight trackers. This is in no small part due to the fact that all three of the U.S. Air Force’s current Boeing 747-based Air Force One aircraft …

absaetze.t: U.S. President Donald Trump’s recent visit to China has drawn particular attention from online flight trackers. This is in no small part due to the fact that all three of the U.S. Air Force’s current Boeing 747-based Air Force One aircraft – the two older VC-25As and the new ex-Qatari VC-25B “Bridge” jet – have supported the trip. Another militarized 747, an E-4B Nightwatch, commonly referred to as a ‘doomsday plane,’ was also spotted shadowing the group to and from Asia.

While this drew a lot of attention online, including blog posts from defense-focused sites, the reality is this is absolutely standard practice. The E-4B is just another part, albeit a very unique and shy one, of the massive aerial logistics ballet that occurs whenever the President leaves the country.

The Air Force currently has four E-4Bs, also known as National Airborne Operations Centers (NAOC), all based at Offutt Air Force Base in Nebraska. Based on the 747-200 model, three of these planes first entered service in the 1970s as E-4A Advanced Airborne Command Posts (AACP). Those aircraft were subsequently brought up to the E-4B NAOC standard in the 1980s, and were eventually joined by a fourth example converted straight to that configuration. The jets have been continuously upgraded over the years. In addition to supporting presidential travel, the Nightwatch aircraft also regularly transport the Secretary of Defense (now also referred to as the Secretary of War) and their staff during overseas trips, among other roles.
The VC-25s carrying Trump and the rest of his entourage left Andrews Air Force Base just outside Washington, D.C., on November 16. An E-4B was tracked heading out from Offutt at around the same time.

Trump headed first for a brief visit to the Philippines before traveling on to China. Plane spotters had a rare opportunity to see all three VC-25s parked together at Ninoy Aquino International Airport in Manila.
The Nightwatch jet headed separately to Kadena Air Base on the Japanese island of Okinawa.
All three VC-25s left China carrying Trump and the rest of the U.S. delegation earlier today. As the trio began to pass over Japan’s home islands, the E-4B took off from Kadena to follow them.

As mentioned at the start, the E-4B shadowing the VC-25s and being forward-deployed in Kadena during Trump’s visit to the Philippines and then China is no surprise. This is standard operating procedure for when the President of the United States travels abroad. Flight trackers notably caught a similar procession of aircraft during Trump’s trip to China back in May.

While the E-4Bs are nowhere near as luxurious as the VC-25As or the new VC-25B, they are just as capable of serving as airborne command posts, if not more so in many respects. They are unofficially referred to as ‘doomsday planes’ because they are specifically configured to provide the president and other senior military officials with a flying headquarters they can use for any and all duties, including directing nuclear strikes during the most serious crises. They are hardened against electromagnetic pulses caused by nuclear detonations and have the ability to stay airborne for days. Their very existence, at least one being on alert at all times to support the National Command Authority, is a critical component that underpins America’s nuclear deterrent. Even if an adversary destroys much of the country, an E-4 can remain airborne to order the counter-attack.

With all this in mind, the E-4B fleet is key to so-called continuity of government plans, which are in place to make sure key elements of the federal government remain functional following an attack or a similarly serious contingency. As a prime example, President George W. Bush rode on one of the VC-25A Air Force One aircraft in the immediate wake of the 9/11 terrorist attacks, but there were discussions about transferring him to a Nightwatch jet. Bush ultimately decided against making the change, but an E-4B was still scrambled and orbited over Washington, D.C., for a time. This is hardly the only time a president has made use of an E-4B, or one of its predecessors, as well as command ships, as TWZ has examined in the past.

Within this broader context, E-4Bs have been a key feature of overseas presidential travel for decades now, although they are the least visible of the presidential aerial armada. This massive airlift and logistics effort includes bringing in multiple examples of the presidential motorcade, Marine One helicopters, and various force protection assets. This involves many sorties by C-17 and C-5 cargo aircraft that cover many thousands of miles each. The videos below from Trump’s visit this week to the Philippines give a sense of just one portion of these options, albeit the most visible one, the vertical airlift component.

Beyond its strategic command and control mission, having an E-4B positioned in the region the president is visiting during overseas trips offers a critical option for refuge and escape, as well as an additional backup aircraft to Air Force One, should any emergencies arise. The exact parameters for where the Nightwatch aircraft go are unknown, but would be based on what suitable airports are available and what potential threats and contingencies could arise. They are never seen at the same locations as Air Force One and are always separated by a distance of dozens of miles, at least, in friendly countries — close enough to be accessed by Marine One in an emergency — or generally in a region for more sensitive locales where such close proximity basing isn’t an option.

E-4Bs do not need to be airborne to act as command and control platforms and secure communications relay nodes, either. This further feeds into their continuity of government role. These are capabilities that can also be made available, if required, to assist the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) during major natural disasters or to help serve as command posts and communications nodes in other emergencies.

The changing character of the Air Force One fleet could put new emphasis on the E-4Bs, as well as the replacement E-4C Survivable Airborne Operations Center (SAOC) jets the Air Force is now in the process of acquiring.

Trump’s trip back from China has notably underscored a significant difference between the VC-25As and the new VC-25B Bridge aircraft, which is that the latter lacks aerial refueling capability. Two fully-outfitted VC-25Bs that Boeing is still in the process of converting for the Air Force will also not be capable of refueling in flight. The E-4Bs can refuel in flight, and the E-4Cs will be able to do so, as well.

TWZ has previously explored the Air Force’s decision to axe the aerial refueling requirement for the VC-25B in detail. The ostensible logic is that the VC-25Bs are based on newer 747-8i aircraft with more capable and fuel-efficient engines than the aging 747-200-based VC-25As. The new aircraft are, as a result, capable of longer unrefueled flights, though maximum range requirements were also watered down.

At the same time, in-flight refueling allows the VC-25As (as well as the E-4Bs) to remain aloft for days at a time. This, in turn, could be critical in a major crisis where access to secure airfields might be limited, if not completely unavailable, for a prolonged period of time.

The VC-25B Bridge jet has prompted a whole new array of operational security questions, which TWZ was calling attention to even before the decision was formally made to outfit it for presidential use. The circumstances of Trump’s return from the NATO summit in Turkey in July had prompted a further flurry of reports about whether the modified, Qatari-gifted jet lacked sufficient defensive features and other capabilities in line with the existing VC-25As. The President had flown to Turkey on the Bridge jet, but was reportedly covertly moved between other aircraft on the way back. This was said to have been done as a security precaution amid then-escalating fighting with Iran.

President Trump subsequently downplayed the series of events, but said that the Bridge aircraft would be sent to have its capabilities “maxed out.” The White House confirmed that the jet would receive “additional upgrades and enhancements,” but did not elaborate. It is unclear how the aircraft’s configuration has changed in the ensuing months.

It is worth noting here that the upgrades in question would have to be limited to defensive systems. The Bridge aircraft could also have entered service without certain communications and networking capabilities found on the VC-25As. Another way to mitigate any such limitations could be to have a VC-25A or an E-4B operating closely enough to establish a line-of-sight data connection relatively quickly so it can leverage the better-equipped aircraft’s communications systems if needed.

As an aside, Trump arrived in China aboard the Bridge aircraft and was seen boarding it to head back to the United States. Reporters onboard had their phones taken away during the return flight for still unexplained security reasons. Fox News has reported that the president is aiming to set a record for the longest continuous flight for an Air Force One aircraft. At the time of writing, its unclear whether the president has touched back down anywhere publicly since leaving Shenzhen.
Where the E-4B is now is also unclear, but it was last tracked continuing along a path shadowing behind Air Force One, where one would expect to see it.

items.titel: Regent Squire Wing-In-Ground Effect Drone To Patrol Middle East Waters
items.anriss: Regent has reached a deal to sell an unspecified number of its autonomous Squire Seagliders to a U.S. government customer, Regent CEO Billy Thalheimer announced on X . The electric-powered drones will make up “a small fleet that will be …

absaetze.t: Regent has reached a deal to sell an unspecified number of its autonomous Squire Seagliders to a U.S. government customer, Regent CEO Billy Thalheimer announced on X. The electric-powered drones will make up “a small fleet that will be deployed in the Middle East next year, doing multi-domain perception” for that customer, Thalheimer stated in his post. He declined to name the customer, the number of drones involved or the value of the contract, and so did the communications arm of his Rhode Island-based company when we asked.
What makes the Squire unique is that it is what is known as a hydrofoiling wing-in-ground (WIG) effect craft.

The WIG drone uses a hydrofoil to get airborne and then cruise in the air at an altitude of about one wingspan above the water. These ground-effect flights are designed to take advantage of the cusion of air compressed between the wings and the surface, providing a sweet spot of increased lift and reduced drag. In theory, this should provide the Squire with high efficiency and relevant speed, all without needing to operate from a traditional runway.

Regent describes the Squire as a “drone that flies in ground effect below radar line of sight at up to 70 knots, with a planned range of more than 100 nautical miles and a 50-pound configurable payload for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR), logistics, search and rescue, and anti-submarine warfare.”

In his post, Thalheimer notes that “combined with various sensors, Squire can do multiple on-water perception and [communications] missions, separated by distances far greater than a USV could quickly cover, all without specialized launch and recovery equipment.”
While flying between sites, “Squire can continue sensing,” he added. “Air and sea: multi-domain perception.”

To make this mission work, “Squire has to operate completely autonomously, which it does running on our in-house vehicle control software,” the CEO continued. “Squire can also be plugged into mission-management and multi-asset coordination autonomy systems, which we’ve already demonstrated with TAK and [Anduril’s] Lattice.”
On the Squire product page, Regent displays a rendering showing how several of these craft could be loaded aboard a transport aircraft.
In a story covering Thalheimer’s remarks at UP Summit in Florida, Aviation Week reported that the CEO said the Squires will perform an “underwater perception” mission.

That’s likely a nod to counter-mine work, which has become a big part of U.S. Central Command’s (CENTCOM) mission in the Middle East as it escorts ships through the Strait of Hormuz and maintains a naval blockade on Iran.

The announcement of the Squire contract comes as the Pentagon said it has surged more than 25,000 unmanned and counter-drone systems to CENTCOM. In addition, CENTCOM, as we previously reported, has established Task Force Falcon Strike, “the first multinational attack drone task force,” according to the command.

The task force will “employ one-way attack drones consisting of unmanned systems from above, on, and below the sea operated by military support staff from the United States and regional partners,” according to CENTCOM.
The command declined to say whether the Squire WIG craft will be part of this effort.

In addition to Squire, Regent is working with the Marine Corps to develop a much larger WIG craft, called the Viceroy Seaglider. It is designed to carry 12 passengers or 3,500 pounds of cargo, all while swiftly skimming the surface of the ocean, allowing it to avoid radar detection.

In September, the company announced announced today it extended its collaboration with the U.S. Marine Corps Warfighting Lab, “adding $5 million in mission dollars and bringing the total value of the partnership to $19.25 million to date.” The goal is to demonstrate “the full-scale Seaglider prototype’s capabilities in operationally relevant environments, alongside advances in command-and-control integration to support how Seagliders would be tasked, tracked, and coordinated within defense operations.”
As we have previously noted, the WIG concept certainly is not new, but prior attempts to employ it on a large scale have generated limited success, particularly for military purposes.
From our prior reporting:

“The Soviet Union remains the most notable operator of military WIG designs, known in Russian as ekranoplans – a term now widely used as a catch-all for WIG designs – but even there their service was limited. Efforts to revive military ekranoplans in Russia in recent years have so far not produced any operational types.”
You can see one of the Soviet Union’s exkranoplans in flight in the following video.
China also has a WIG craft, dubbed the “Bohai Sea Monster,’” and it was spotted in May with apparent weapons hardpoints, suggesting that it has a combat role.

The Squire would not be the first WIG craft to operate in the Middle East in recent decades. Iran too has operated many small WIG craft called the Bavar-2. It was designed primarily as a low-signature scout and patrol platform and was featured multiple times in IRGC propaganda videos. It is somewhat ironic that what was once a staple of the IRGC Navy is now being deployed in an unmanned fashion against it. We have seen similar development with one-way attack munitions, for instance.
Meanwhile, last year, the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) completed the Liberty Lifter program without developing an aircraft. It was an effort to create a large WIG craft.
Given how unique it will be for a WIG craft to be operational in a combat setting, we will keep an eye on how this contract develops and provide updates when warranted.

items.titel: Emily Carr and E.J. Hughes lead the way at Heffel's $10m autumn auctions
items.anriss: The Canadian auction house’s marquee autumnal sales in Toronto also saw strong results for works by William Kurelek and Ivan Eyre, landscape painters from the Prairies

absaetze.t: The Heffel Fine Art Auction House held its marquee autumn evening sales on Wednesday (18 November) in Toronto, attracting a packed house of bidders and spectators to the city’s swank Yorkville district and generating C$14.4m ($10m) in sales, works by Canadian masters taking top dollar. As things got underway, a Heffel representative noted that any US tariffs were “the responsibility of the buyer”, a reflection of these often-testy times.

“At a time of strong national pride, it is especially meaningful to see collectors celebrating Canada’s artistic achievements and our distinct national culture,” David Heffel, the auction house’s president, said at the end of the evening.

The back-to-back sales (41 lots of post-war and contemporary art followed by 47 works of Canadian, Impressionist and modern art) got off to a flying start when a watercolour by the Vancouver-born artist E.J. Hughes hammered for C$475,000 ($331,700)—nearly 12 times its high estimate. Titled Wharves at Chemainus (2000) and depicting the titular logging community on Vancouver Island, the painting is modest in size at 20in by 24in; with fees, the price came to C$571,250 ($398,900).

Hughes had made waves at Heffel’s auctions last spring, when his Coastal Boats Near Sidney, BC realised a whoppingC$5.7m ($4.1m), including fees. Several more Hughes works were up for sale Wednesday night including two that significantly outperformer their estimates: The Hope River at Chilliwack, BC (1961), which took in C$253,250 ($176,800) with fees; and The Freighter “World Ares” at Crofton (1980), which hauled in C$229,250 ($160,000) including fees.

The second sale’s cover lot, Emily Carr’s luminous canvas Alert Bay (with Welcome Figure) (around 1912), brought C$1.3m ($922,000) including fees, comfortably within its estimate. It was the only seven-figure result of the night. Some of the proceeds from its sale will benefit the Audain Art Museum in Whistler, British Columbia, where it was shown in the context of a major traveling exhibition of Carr’s work in 2019-20.

A work on paper by the Carr, Music in the Trees (around 1935), topped its high estimate to achieve an impressive C$421,250 ($294,100) with fees. In all, six works by the Victoria-born artist were sold at Heffel on Wednesday night, fetching a combined, fee-inclusive total of C$2.5m ($1.7m).

A handful of works by Jean Paul Riopelle were on offer during the post-war and contemporary portion of the night, generating around C$1.3m ($907,800) in sales. His large-scale, wintry abstraction Herbeuse (1967),proved particularly appealing. Swift bidding pushed it to around double its high estimate. With fees, the price came to C$571,250 ($398,900). It was shown in the Carnegie International the year Riopelle painted it, and later in Paris, where the Montréal-born artist, a master of the palette knife, spent decades. The work with the highest estimate in the post-war and contemporary sale, Riopelle’s Brumaire (1953), was expected to bring between C$1.5m and C$2m, but failed to sell.

Among the night’s other big-ticket items was Paul-Émile Borduas’s oil painting Empâtement (1957), from the artist’s black-and-white period—and punctuated with splashes of red. It realised C$841,250 with fees ($587,400), easily topping its high estimate of C$500,000. It had been acquired directly from the artist by London’s Arthur Tooth & Sons gallery in 1957 and, more recently, was in the collection of Québecois lyricist and songwriter Luc Plamondon.

J.E.H. MacDonald’s oil sketch Magnetawan River Rapids (1912), a preparatory work for a major canvas that is in the collection of the Art Gallery of Hamilton, achieved C$451,250 with fees ($315,000), tripling its high estimate of C$150,000.

Arguably the surprise of the night was Ivan Eyre (1935-2022), who was long a professor at the University of Manitoba and is best known for his prairie landscapes. His intensely autumnal acrylic-on-canvas landscape Golden Rod (1981) realised C$391,250 with fees ($273,200), more than tripling its high estimate of C$120,000 while setting a new auction record for the artist. That record was smashed in turn just one lot later, when Eyre’s Yellow Wood (around 1995) realised C$481,250 with fees ($336,000), five times its high estimate of C$90,000.

The beloved William Kurelek, who was raised on a farm near Winnipeg, also made a splash.His snowy landscape painting I Knew How the Clouds Arise (1969), which was featured on the cover of the catalogue for the artist’s first retrospective in 1970, realised C$313,250 including fees ($218,700), just over its high estimate, while the evocative campfire scene Wiener Roast on My Father’s Farm (1974), exceeded expectations to sell for C$265,250 with fees ($185,200).

items.titel: Drawing Center's Laura Hoptman Wins Curatorial Excellence Award
items.anriss: Art Movements, published every Thursday afternoon, is a roundup of must-know news, appointments, awards, and other happenings in today’s chaotic art world.

absaetze.t: Plus: Joyce Awards winners announced, Agnes Gund's gift to art in schools, and Derrick Adams and LEGO make a splash in Miami.

Art Movements, published every Thursday afternoon, is a roundup of must-know news, appointments, awards, and other happenings in today’s chaotic art world.
Laura Hoptman Wins CCS Bard Audrey Irmas Award for Curatorial Excellence

The Center for Curatorial Studies at Bard College announced Laura Hoptman, executive director of the Drawing Center in New York, as the recipient of the 2027 Audrey Irmas Award for Curatorial Excellence, a $25,000 prize. Hoptman's curriculum vitae reads like a roll call of NYC's major institutions: She started out as an assistant curator at the Bronx Museum in the 1980s and later held curatorial roles at the Museum of Modern Art and the New Museum.
So it is no surprise that, when asked what this recognition signified for her, Hoptman chose to invoke the network and community that her career has grown alongside.

“The best kind of professional recognition comes from one's peers, and this is one of the many reasons why this award is so meaningful to me,” Hoptman told Hyperallergic in an email. “It also reminds me how damn lucky I have been to have spent the last 30 years around art and artists in one of the greatest cultural hubs in the world. After all this time, my vocation still fills me with joy.”

items.titel: The Ebullient Ecofeminism of Carolina Caycedo
items.anriss: ST LOUIS, MO — A pink lake under an avalanche of digital detritus; a neon rainbow behind a man in a hazmat suit; a gilt sky above a lone wind turbine. These are among the surreal, meticulously rendered scenes in Carolina Caycedo’s series …

absaetze.t: Her candy-colored drawings lure the eye only to disquiet the mind, exposing the contradictions of so-called clean energy.
November 19, 2026 — 2 min read

ST LOUIS, MO — A pink lake under an avalanche of digital detritus; a neon rainbow behind a man in a hazmat suit; a gilt sky above a lone wind turbine. These are among the surreal, meticulously rendered scenes in Carolina Caycedo’s series Mineral Intensive (2023–ongoing).

Caycedo’s candy-colored drawings lure the eye only to disquiet the mind, exposing the contradictions of so-called clean energy, whose production often depends on environmentally destructive mineral extraction.

Such visual beguilement — and ecological exigency — anchors Carolina Caycedo: Growing Deep Roots, an exhibition of sculpture, video, printmaking, and drawing that explores the joyous, multisensory dimensions of the artist’s activism.

Born and raised in Bogotá, Colombia, the Los Angeles-based artist devoted two years to collaborative research with botanists, plant taxonomists, and Native elders, informing her rendering of prairie and botanical life across the Mississippi River watershed. By turns bright and delicate, Caycedo’s Plant Portraits series (2021–ongoing) lends an ecofeminist bent to the larger show, merging feminine anatomy with botanical illustration.

Like a heavenly necklace, “Celestial Autonomy, the Dance of Big Dipper and North Star” (2023) dangles in the center of the gallery. Constructed of Alaskan nets, buoys, and other fishing equipment — its title honors the indigenous communities in the region.

Across the Mississippi River, another sculptural installation, “Fiesta de la Raíces” (2026), vivifies the National Building Arts Center in Sauget, Illinois. A three-dimensional “portrait” of the area’s root systems, the sculpture resembles a shaggy chandelier of rope, beads, and natural fibers — beckoning admirers to bask in its festive opulence.

At a time when ecological disaster feels ever imminent, art attuned to earthly precarity can often feel didactic or downright drab. Caycedo insists on an alternate vision: Humanity in sync with a resplendent planet — the ground beneath us trembling with riches, the sky adorned with unseen stars.

Carolina Caycedo: Growing Deep Roots continues at the Kemper Art Museum at Washington University in St. Louis (One Brookings Drive, St. Louis, Missouri) through January 4, and at the National Building Arts Center (NBAC) (2300 Falling Springs Road, Sauget, Illinois) through December 12. The exhibition was curated by Meredith Malone and James McAnally.

items.titel: Cosentino supports architectural creativity with Ēclos mineral surface
items.anriss: Cosentino aims to put the creative freedom of architects and designers front and centre with its Ēclos surface, designed for three-dimensional compositions with refined edges, corners and waterfall ends.

absaetze.t: Cosentino aims to put the creative freedom of architects and designers front and centre with its Ēclos surface, designed for three-dimensional compositions with refined edges, corners and waterfall ends.
Ēclos is the Spanish brand’s latest mineral surface material, made with advanced methods to emulate the look of natural stone and be free of crystalline silica.
The surface is made with Cosentino’s proprietary Inlayr manufacturing process, which makes the rich and naturalistic veining run through the slab.
This gives Ēclos a premium look, Cosentino explained, and makes it a fitting constituent for the most sophisticated interiors.
According to Cosentino, it is in the junctions and details that a kitchen or room feels resolved and where its architectural character emerges.

“For architects and designers, the section deserves as much consideration as the elevation,” said the company. “The placement of a joint, the treatment of an edge and the relationship between adjoining surfaces shape how a material is perceived.”
“These details establish the architectural language of an element, whether the intention is to suggest a continuous volume or to make its assembly visible.”

Although surfaces are often selected based on their colour or pattern, Cosentino says that full-body design should be just as crucial a consideration, allowing exposed edges and transitions between levels or materials to contribute to building a coherent form.

“With Ēclos, the patterning is constructed within the slab rather than confined to its face,” continued the brand. “That makes the relationship between surface and depth an important part of the design conversation, particularly where edges remain visible.”
“The interest lies not just in the appearance of the material, but in how it can be cut, assembled and brought into a project with adjacent finishes.”
Its fabricators can advise how cutting, profiling, jointing and installation can help a designer’s vision come together.
The process can involve reviewing samples, fabrication drawings and, where appropriate, physical mock-ups.
“The position of a seam or the treatment of an exposed edge can subtly alter the proportions and perceived weight of an element,” said Cosentino.
“The aim is not necessarily to make every joint disappear, but to make each one deliberate.”
“Whether the intention is a continuous volume or a clearly expressed assembly, the junction deserves as much consideration as the surface itself,” the brand continued.
Ēclos launched earlier this year and joins an expanding portfolio of low-silica, high-recycled mineral surface worktops from Cosentino, including Silestone, Dekton and Sensa.
It is suitable for both residential and commercial environments and can be used on worktops, splashbacks, walls and other surfaces.
The first Ēclos collection – Eclectic Veins – incorporates 10 stone-like designs, ranging from ice-white styles to dramatic darks, all made with a minimum of 50 per cent recycled content.
The material is practical for everyday use, withstanding scratches and stains, and is easy to clean and maintain.
It is also resistant to temperatures of up to 220 degrees Celsius, including contact with hot cookware.
To learn more about Cosentino and Ēclos, visit the company’s website.
